name: Karl Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and have answered calls and chats at the contact centre for years. I finished secondary school and can handle the usual delivery complaint at the pace of most experienced agents, though I do not run a team. The pay is low for this work. I never use AI tools; I would rather check the order line and read the delivery date to the customer myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you think about when you leave?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Meera works irregular hours selling tickets at a bus station, and our grown children have homes of their own. We rent our flat and have about three weeks of expenses saved. Few other centres are nearby. I hope I can ease back from full-time work someday, but I have no settled wage replacement; I like a call that ends with the parcel actually found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the desk AI Plateau sounds like another neat note, while the actual order still needs checking. I would keep reading the delivery date back before I close a call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my usual calls remain, but three weeks saved is not much if Meera loses a ticket shift. The rent due next month worries me even when the machine changes little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking delivery complaints and checking the order by hand. In the first year of small change, I’d ask the supervisor for one extra paid Saturday shift a month if the queue needs cover, then set that extra pay aside for rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady about the job, tense about our cash. A quiet AI year still has a rent date every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What order detail helped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Friday a customer’s parcel was scanned at the wrong entrance. I found the building number in the paper delivery note before calling the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to extra shift pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Meera (my wife) and I would leave any extra shift pay in a separate rent envelope. Our grown children have bills of their own.

say: I’d say **order records** still matter in AI Plateau.
I’d read the **delivery date** back before closing calls.
think: I still worry **three weeks saved** cannot absorb a missed ticket shift.
do: Keep handling **delivery complaints** and checking original orders by hand in 2026.
Ask for one **paid Saturday shift** monthly if cover is needed and save its extra pay for rent.
S0.quote: A quiet AI year still has a rent date every month.
fieldNote: A **wrong entrance scan** was corrected from the order note.
The **three-week reserve** makes even AI Plateau financially tense.
He saves **extra shift pay** only if a paid shift is offered.

steps.text: Keep taking delivery complaints and check original order dates by hand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption can take the short delivery questions before anyone gives a worker notice. I would ask the supervisor for a written paid rota and a person customers can call when a machine sends them to the wrong address.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my years on the desk might help with complaints, but fewer paid hours would put our rent in trouble. Meera’s station shifts move around, and there are few other centres to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d attend a required demonstration of the new delivery-answer system on paid time only if a trainer walks me through real wrong-address cases. In the first year simple chats move, I’d compare the old and new paid rotas and apply for a posted paid counter role only if my hours fall and its written weekly wage and hours cover rent and utilities; I’d keep my current shifts until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about pay, uneasy about learning from a screen. A required demonstration after my shift would be another unpaid hour of worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trainer show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring a wrong-address case and ask the trainer to show where the system got its date. I need to see the mistake in a real call before I use the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare counter pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the full week’s counter wage, not just one tempting hourly rate. The rent needs a month of paid days.

I’d demand a **human correction route** for wrong addresses.

I know **few nearby centres** limit quick job choices.
do: Attend a **required paid-time demonstration** only if a trainer shows real wrong-address cases in 2026.
Compare **paid rotas** before and after simple chats move.
Apply after **call-hour cuts** for posted paid counter work only with written rent-and-utilities-covering weekly wage and hours; stay until signed offer.
feel: **Anxious** about pay, uneasy learning a new screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the other agents AGI by 2028 could answer most delivery complaints and check the address without us. I would ask for written dates of paid shift changes and posted paid openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my ordinary calls could disappear in 2028. Robots around 2031 come later for physical work, but three weeks saved cannot pay rent while I search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d stop the planned replacement of our working dining chairs and keep the money for the next rent bill. In the first year after 2028, if calls are cut, I’d apply for a posted paid parcel-counter job only if written weekly wage and hours cover rent and utilities; I’d keep present paid calls until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but I can still ask for a real posting. Three weeks of savings is shorter than the time it takes to hear back from most jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the parcel posting show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the parcel shop what a full paid week actually looks like. A vacancy with two afternoon shifts will not meet our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can the chairs safely wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Meera (my wife) and I can keep the old chairs while they are safe to use. We need the replacement money for the flat this month.

say: I’d request **written shift dates** and posted paid openings before the contact centre cuts hours.
I’d warn colleagues **2028 AGI** could take ordinary delivery complaints that pay our wages.
think: I think my **ordinary calls** could disappear.
I know **three weeks saved** cannot carry a long search.
I know **2031 robots** arrive later than thinking AI.
do: Delay **chair replacement** in 2026 only while old chairs are safe, retaining planned money for the next rent bill.
After 2028 call cuts, apply for **posted paid parcel work** only with written wage and hours covering rent and utilities.
Keep **present paid calls** until a suitable parcel offer is signed.
feel: **Alarmed**, still able to ask for real terms.
S2.quote: Three weeks of savings is shorter than the time it takes to hear back from most jobs.
fieldNote: The **chair deferral** requires safe old furniture.
He needs the **full paid week**, not two token shifts.
Thinking AI arrives in **2028**, before physical robots.

steps.text: Delay chair replacement only while old chairs remain safe; retain money for rent
Apply after cuts for posted parcel job with written rent-and-utilities-covering wage and hours
Keep paid calls until suitable parcel offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives time to see which parcel-counter jobs remain paid. I would ask the manager for a posted wage before treating a course flyer as a route to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years could help me learn a new counter, but full AGI may also answer its customers. Robots around 2034 come later; I cannot afford a long unpaid classroom stretch now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d keep taking paid delivery calls and ask a parcel manager what the job and any training actually require. In the first year after 2031, if call hours fall, I’d apply for a posted paid parcel role only if its written weekly wage and hours cover rent and utilities, keeping present calls until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with enough time to check a vacancy before moving. A course flyer is paper until there is a paying job behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask about training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how many hours a new counter worker is paid while learning the parcel system. I have not agreed to a course; I need the vacancy and wage first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What wage figure matters at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Meera (my wife) and I would compare the full weekly pay with rent and utilities. We cannot make up a missing wage by calling a course an investment.

I’d question whether **parcel work** remains paid after 2031.

I know **2031 AGI** could reach that work too.
I cannot afford **unpaid classroom weeks** now.
do: Keep **paid delivery calls** and ask parcel manager about posted job, training and paid learning hours from 2026.
After 2031 cuts, apply for **posted paid parcel work** only with written rent-and-utilities-covering weekly wage and hours; keep calls until signed offer.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to inspect a real vacancy.
S3.quote: A course flyer is paper until there is a paying job behind it.
fieldNote: His **course inquiry** is information gathering, not enrollment or refusal.

steps.text: Keep paid delivery calls; ask parcel manager about posted job, training and paid learning hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives years to keep a paid delivery desk while workers learn which jobs remain. I would ask for a yearly paid-hours plan, not a count of answered chats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I may be closer to fewer working hours then, but I do not know what income would replace this wage. Three weeks saved makes the next rent bill more real than a distant retirement story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking paid calls and ask the supervisor each year for written paid hours. In the first year after 2036, if my shifts fall, I’d apply for posted paid reception work only if written weekly wage and hours cover rent and utilities; I’d leave current calls only after a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watchful about the distant change, anxious about this month’s bills. Ten years before AGI reaches my calls cannot pay the rent due next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare in reception?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare a whole paid week in reception with what the contact centre pays. A higher hourly rate for two shifts would still be a cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have their own households. Meera (my wife) and I will make a plan from wages we know, not an assumed pension or their pay.

I’d ask for **paid shift counts**, not only totals of answered customer chats.
think: I think I may want **fewer hours** later.
I cannot assume a **replacement income** without evidence.
I still worry about **next week’s rent**.
do: Keep **paid calls** and ask yearly for written shift hours from 2026.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could take ordinary delivery calls before I can build even another month of savings. Three weeks saved will not carry rent through a long search. Written paid-hour notice and a real posted job with weekly wages and hours covering rent and utilities would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a customer can speak to the person who found the parcel. My father kept every delivery slip until the buyer had the right box in hand.

headlineQuote: My father kept every delivery slip until the buyer had the right box in hand.
portrait: At **58**, Karl is an experienced average-skill agent after secondary school with lower pay.
He and Meera rent with **three weeks saved** and few nearby centres.
He never uses **AI tools**, preferring order records and spoken dates.
He needs **paid hours** while working toward an uncertain later life.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could take ordinary calls before he can grow savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid-hour notice** and posted rent-covering work would help.
